dx: Atopic dermatitis complicated by molluscum contagiosum
case: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of an itchy rash that has been present since infancy and new bumps on his trunk for 2 months. As an infant, he had red, oozing patches on his cheeks and the extensor surfaces of his arms and legs. His father has asthma, and his mother has allergic rhinitis. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows dry skin and thickened, lichenified plaques with excoriations in the antecubital and popliteal fossae. Several dozen firm, flesh-colored, dome-shaped papules 2 to 4 mm in diameter with central umbilication are present on the trunk and in the antecubital fossae, and some are arranged in lines along scratch marks. Diagnosis: atopic dermatitis complicated by molluscum contagiosum.

questions.stem: Two months later, he is brought to the emergency department because of fever and painful skin lesions for 2 days. His temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F). Physical examination shows clusters of uniform, punched-out erosions with hemorrhagic crusts over the eczematous plaques of his neck and arms. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these new lesions?
options: Staphylococcus aureus
Varicella zoster virus
Herpes simplex virus
Streptococcus pyogenes
approach: Key clue: uniform, punched-out erosions clustered on top of eczema in a febrile child.
This pattern is eczema herpeticum, a herpes simplex infection that spreads across skin with a broken barrier.
Atopic skin is prone to it because the barrier is damaged and Th2 cytokines lower the skin's own antimicrobial peptides.
questions.why: Eczema herpeticum is herpes simplex virus (usually type 1) spreading rapidly through eczematous skin. It shows up as many monomorphic vesicles that quickly become punched-out erosions with hemorrhagic crusts, often with fever. Atopic skin is vulnerable because filaggrin loss weakens the barrier, and IL-4 and IL-13 from Th2 cells reduce keratinocyte production of antimicrobial peptides such as cathelicidin and defensins. It is a dermatologic urgency because the virus can spread to the eye or disseminate.
whyNot: Staphylococcus aureus colonizes most atopic skin and causes weeping, honey-crusted impetiginization of eczema. It does not produce uniform punched-out erosions.
Primary varicella appears in crops over the whole body, most densely on the trunk, with lesions in different stages at once. It does not concentrate on eczematous plaques.
Correct.
Streptococcus pyogenes causes impetigo with honey-colored crusts or cellulitis with spreading warm erythema, not clusters of uniform punched-out erosions.

questions.stem: Genetic testing shows that he is heterozygous for a loss-of-function mutation in the filaggrin gene (FLG). His father carries the same mutation and has fine white scale on both shins and accentuated palmar creases. Which of the following best explains how this mutation weakens the epidermal barrier in both patients?
options: Defective keratin bundling and less natural moisturizing factor
Failure to remove sulfate from cholesterol sulfate in the cornified layer
Weak keratin 5 and 14 filaments in basal keratinocytes
Loss of E-cadherin adhesion between spinous layer cells
approach: The father's fine scale on the shins with prominent palmar creases is ichthyosis vulgaris, which shares FLG mutations with atopic dermatitis.
Filaggrin comes from profilaggrin in keratohyalin granules of the stratum granulosum.
It aggregates keratin filaments into a tight cornified layer and is then broken down into natural moisturizing factor that keeps the stratum corneum hydrated.
questions.why: Filaggrin is made as profilaggrin in the keratohyalin granules of the stratum granulosum. It bundles keratin filaments so corneocytes flatten into a tight, tough layer, and its breakdown products (amino acids and urocanic acid) form natural moisturizing factor, which holds water and keeps the surface slightly acidic. Loss-of-function FLG mutations leave a dry, leaky stratum corneum. That causes ichthyosis vulgaris, which is semidominant, and is the strongest genetic risk factor for atopic dermatitis because allergens and microbes can get through the barrier.
whyNot: Correct.
This is steroid sulfatase deficiency, the cause of X-linked ichthyosis. Cholesterol sulfate builds up and corneocytes fail to shed, giving large dark scales in boys. It does not involve filaggrin.
Mutations in keratins 5 and 14 make basal keratinocytes fragile and cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex, with blisters from friction rather than dry scaling skin.
E-cadherin forms adherens junctions between keratinocytes. Its loss is not the mechanism of filaggrin-related barrier failure.

topics: Filaggrin and the stratum corneum barrier

questions.stem: His mother asks why some of the papules on his trunk are arranged in straight lines. Which of the following best explains this arrangement?
options: Viral spread along a sensory dermatome
Lymphatic spread from a primary papule
Contact with a plant resin while playing
Autoinoculation of virus by scratching
approach: Identify the papules: firm, flesh-colored, umbilicated domes in a young child are molluscum contagiosum.
Molluscum spreads by direct skin contact and by autoinoculation.
Scratching itchy eczema carries virus from a lesion along the scratch line, so new papules form in a row.
questions.why: Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection of keratinocytes that produces firm, flesh-colored, dome-shaped papules with a central dimple. It spreads by skin-to-skin contact, shared objects, and autoinoculation, and in adults it can spread by sexual contact. Children with atopic dermatitis often have many lesions because they scratch and their barrier is weak, and scratching drags virus along the skin so papules line up. In healthy children the lesions resolve on their own over months. Very numerous or large lesions in an adult suggest HIV infection.
whyNot: A dermatomal band of grouped vesicles on a red base is herpes zoster, from reactivation in a sensory ganglion. Molluscum does not live in nerves.
Nodules that climb up a limb along lymphatics are typical of sporotrichosis after a thorn injury. Molluscum stays within the epidermis.
Linear streaks after brushing against a plant are typical of allergic contact dermatitis to urushiol, which gives itchy vesicles, not umbilicated papules.
Correct.

topics: Molluscum in atopic dermatitis and HIV

questions.stem: One papule is removed by curettage. Microscopy shows large, eosinophilic inclusion bodies within the cytoplasm of the infected keratinocytes. Which of the following features of the causative virus best explains the location of these inclusions?
options: Integration of the viral genome into host chromosomes
Replication of its DNA genome in the cytoplasm
Nuclear transcription by host RNA polymerase II
Reverse transcription of an RNA genome into DNA
approach: The inclusions are molluscum bodies, the hallmark of molluscum contagiosum, a poxvirus.
Poxviruses are large, enveloped dsDNA viruses that carry their own DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
Because they bring their own enzymes, they replicate entirely in the cytoplasm, so viral factories form cytoplasmic inclusions.
questions.why: Poxviruses, including molluscum contagiosum virus, are the only DNA viruses that replicate in the cytoplasm. They carry their own DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and other enzymes in the virion, so they do not need the host nucleus. Viral assembly sites fill the keratinocyte cytoplasm and form large eosinophilic molluscum (Henderson-Patterson) bodies. Human papillomavirus, the cause of warts, is a nonenveloped circular dsDNA virus that replicates in the nucleus and produces koilocytes with wrinkled nuclei and a perinuclear halo.
whyNot: Integration into host DNA is a feature of retroviruses and of high-risk HPV in cancers. It does not create cytoplasmic inclusions.
Correct.
Most DNA viruses, such as HPV and herpesviruses, transcribe their genes in the nucleus with host RNA polymerase II, giving nuclear changes. Poxviruses avoid the nucleus.
Reverse transcription is used by retroviruses and hepatitis B virus. Molluscum contagiosum virus has a DNA genome and no reverse transcriptase.

dx: Allergic contact dermatitis from poison oak (urushiol)
case: A 34-year-old man who works on a trail maintenance crew comes to urgent care because of an intensely itchy rash on his forearms and shins for 2 days. Four days ago, he spent a day cutting back brush that included poison oak while wearing a short-sleeved shirt. He had a similar rash after trail work last summer. He takes no medications. His temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 74/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows erythematous papules and vesicles arranged in linear streaks on the dorsal forearms, wrists, and anterior shins, with a few tense bullae. There are no mucosal lesions. Diagnosis: allergic contact dermatitis to urushiol from poison oak.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the 2-day delay between his exposure to poison oak and the onset of his rash?
options: Degranulation of IgE-coated dermal mast cells
Recruitment of sensitized memory T cells
Deposition of immune complexes in dermal venules
Direct toxic injury to keratinocytes by the resin
approach: He reacted after a prior exposure last summer, so he was already sensitized.
Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity.
Memory T cells must be recruited to the skin, recognize hapten-modified proteins, and release cytokines, which takes about 48 to 72 hours.
questions.why: Urushiol is a hapten. It binds skin proteins, and at first exposure Langerhans cells carry the modified proteins to lymph nodes to sensitize T cells. On re-exposure, memory T cells travel to the skin, recognize the antigen, and release cytokines such as IFN-gamma that recruit more cells and injure keratinocytes. Recruiting and activating these cells takes time, so the eruption appears about 48 to 72 hours after contact. Irritant contact dermatitis, in contrast, needs no sensitization and appears soon after direct damage.
whyNot: IgE on mast cells mediates type I reactions such as hives and anaphylaxis, which start within minutes of exposure.
Correct.
Immune complex deposition (type III) causes vasculitis or serum sickness. It is not the mechanism of a plant contact rash.
Direct chemical damage is irritant contact dermatitis. It does not need prior sensitization, and his reaction does.

questions.stem: A punch biopsy specimen is obtained from the edge of a vesicle on his forearm. Which of the following histologic findings is most likely?
options: Suprabasal acantholysis above an intact basal row
Subepidermal cleft with many eosinophils
Regular acanthosis with confluent parakeratosis
Intercellular edema within the spinous layer
approach: Allergic contact dermatitis is an eczematous (spongiotic) dermatitis.
Cytokines from T cells make fluid collect between keratinocytes, stretching the desmosomes apart so cells look spongy.
When the fluid pools, it forms intraepidermal vesicles, which match his clinical vesicles.
questions.why: Spongiosis is edema between keratinocytes in the spinous layer. The fluid widens the spaces between cells until the desmosomal connections look like sponge fibers, and pockets of fluid form intraepidermal vesicles. It is the histologic hallmark of acute eczematous dermatitis, including allergic contact dermatitis, with a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate below. Linear streaks of vesicles on exposed skin point to a plant brushing across the skin, while nickel causes rashes on the earlobes or wrist, and wet work gives hand dermatitis.
whyNot: Suprabasal acantholysis with a row of basal cells left on the floor is pemphigus vulgaris, caused by antibodies against desmoglein 3.
A subepidermal blister rich in eosinophils is bullous pemphigoid, an autoimmune disease of older adults.
Regular acanthosis with parakeratosis is the chronic hyperproliferative pattern of psoriasis.
Correct.

questions.stem: During his first exposure last summer, urushiol bound to skin proteins and was taken up by an antigen-presenting cell that resides in the epidermis. Electron microscopy of this cell type would most likely show which of the following?
options: Tennis racket-shaped Birbeck granules
Melanosomes in various stages of maturation
Dense-core granules facing a nerve terminal
Metachromatic granules containing histamine
approach: The antigen-presenting cell of the epidermis is the Langerhans cell, found mostly in the stratum spinosum.
Langerhans cells come from the bone marrow, express CD1a and langerin, and capture antigens that enter the skin.
Their ultrastructural marker is the Birbeck granule, a rod-shaped organelle with a bulb at one end.
questions.why: Langerhans cells are dendritic cells of bone marrow origin that sit in the spinous layer and extend processes between keratinocytes. They take up haptens and other antigens, then migrate to lymph nodes to present them to T cells, which is how sensitization to urushiol or nickel occurs. They stain for CD1a and S-100, and on electron microscopy they contain Birbeck granules, which are rod-shaped and often look like tennis rackets. The other dendritic-looking cells of the epidermis have different jobs and different granules.
whyNot: Correct.
Melanosomes are made by melanocytes, which arise from neural crest, sit in the basal layer, and pass pigment to keratinocytes. Melanocytes do not present antigen.
Dense-core granules next to a nerve ending are typical of Merkel cells, the touch receptors of the basal layer.
Histamine-filled metachromatic granules belong to mast cells, which live in the dermis and drive type I reactions.

questions.stem: After capturing the urushiol-modified proteins during his first exposure, the antigen-presenting cells left the epidermis. To which of the following sites did they most likely migrate to activate naive T cells?
options: Germinal center of a lymph node follicle
Medullary cords of a regional lymph node
Paracortex of a regional lymph node
Periarteriolar sheath of the splenic white pulp
approach: Antigen from the skin is carried by Langerhans cells through afferent lymphatics, not the blood.
Dendritic cells deliver antigen to the zone where naive T cells gather.
In lymph nodes, naive T cells are concentrated in the paracortex, so that is where priming happens.
questions.why: When keratinocytes are stressed, they release IL-1 and TNF and act as part of innate defense. These signals help Langerhans cells mature after they capture antigen. The cells then travel through afferent lymphatics to the draining lymph node, guided by the chemokine receptor CCR7, and settle in the paracortex, the T cell zone. There they present peptide on MHC molecules with costimulation to naive T cells. The primed effector and memory T cells later return to the skin, which is why a second exposure causes the rash.
whyNot: Germinal centers in follicles are where activated B cells proliferate and undergo class switching. Naive T cell priming happens in the T cell zone.
Medullary cords hold plasma cells and macrophages near the exit of the node. They are not the T cell priming zone.
Correct.
The splenic periarteriolar sheath is a T cell zone, but the spleen filters blood-borne antigen. Skin antigens drain by lymphatics to regional nodes.

dx: Erythema multiforme minor after recurrent herpes labialis
case: A 22-year-old woman comes to student health because of a rash on her hands and forearms for 3 days. Ten days ago, she had a painful cold sore on her lower lip that has now crusted. She has had two similar rashes in the past 2 years, each after a cold sore. She takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows symmetric, fixed, round lesions 1 to 2 cm in diameter on the palms, dorsal hands, and extensor forearms. Each lesion has a dusky center, a pale edematous ring, and an outer erythematous ring. Two shallow erosions are present on the buccal mucosa. Nikolsky sign is negative. Diagnosis: erythema multiforme minor triggered by recurrent herpes labialis.

questions.stem: A punch biopsy specimen is obtained from the center of a lesion on her hand. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Neutrophils in venule walls with karyorrhectic debris
Spongiosis forming intraepidermal vesicles
Band-like lymphocytes with sawtooth rete ridges
Interface dermatitis with necrotic keratinocytes
approach: Target lesions with a dusky center after herpes labialis are erythema multiforme.
The reaction is driven by cytotoxic T cells that attack keratinocytes expressing herpes simplex antigens.
T cells gather along the dermal-epidermal junction (interface) and kill keratinocytes, and the dead cells make the center dusky.
questions.why: Erythema multiforme is a cell-mediated reaction, most often to herpes simplex virus and less often to Mycoplasma pneumoniae or drugs. Viral DNA fragments are carried to the skin, and cytotoxic T cells attack keratinocytes expressing viral antigen. Biopsy shows a lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermal-epidermal junction with vacuolar change of the basal layer and scattered necrotic (apoptotic) keratinocytes. Clinically, the lesions are fixed acral targets, and mucosal involvement is absent or limited to the mouth in the minor form.
whyNot: Neutrophils destroying venule walls with nuclear dust is leukocytoclastic vasculitis, which presents as palpable purpura.
Spongiosis with vesicles is the eczematous pattern of contact and atopic dermatitis, which presents as itchy, ill-defined patches.
A band of lymphocytes with sawtooth rete ridges is lichen planus, which presents as flat purple papules without targets.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her 21-year-old roommate began taking lamotrigine 2 weeks ago. She now has fever, painful hemorrhagic crusting of the lips, conjunctivitis, and dusky macules with flaccid blisters on her face and trunk. Light lateral pressure shears off the epidermis. The detached epidermis covers about 8% of her body surface area. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in the roommate?
options: Erythema multiforme major
Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Toxic epidermal necrolysis
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
approach: A new anticonvulsant, fever, two or more mucosal sites, and sheets of detaching skin point to Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis.
These are one disease graded by the area of epidermal detachment.
Under 10% of body surface is Stevens-Johnson syndrome, 10 to 30% is overlap, and over 30% is toxic epidermal necrolysis. At 8% this is Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
questions.why: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are severe drug reactions in which cytotoxic T cells cause widespread keratinocyte death and full-thickness epidermal necrosis. Common triggers include sulfonamides, anticonvulsants (lamotrigine, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol, usually 1 to 4 weeks after starting the drug. Patients have fever, painful mucosal erosions at several sites, and a positive Nikolsky sign. The two names describe the same process, separated by the percentage of body surface that detaches.
whyNot: Erythema multiforme major has typical raised acral target lesions with mucosal involvement, usually after herpes simplex. It does not cause widespread sheets of detaching skin after a new drug.
Correct.
Toxic epidermal necrolysis requires detachment of more than 30% of body surface area. Her 8% is below that.
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome causes a superficial split from an exfoliative toxin in young children and spares the mucosa. This patient has prominent mucosal disease after a drug.

topics: Stevens-Johnson syndrome versus toxic epidermal necrolysis
Drugs that trigger severe skin reactions

questions.stem: Between episodes of herpes labialis, the virus that triggers her rash persists in which of the following?
options: Basal keratinocytes at the vermilion border
Memory B cells in cervical lymph nodes
Sensory neurons of the trigeminal ganglion
Lower motor neurons of the facial nucleus
approach: Recurrent cold sores are caused by herpes simplex virus type 1, an enveloped dsDNA virus.
After the first infection of the lip epithelium, the virus enters sensory nerve endings and travels by retrograde axonal transport to the cell body.
The lip is supplied by the trigeminal nerve, so the virus stays latent in the trigeminal ganglion and reactivates down the same nerve.
questions.why: Herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus infect epithelium first, then enter sensory nerve endings and move to the neuron cell bodies in sensory ganglia. There the viral genome persists as an episome with very limited gene expression, hidden from the immune system. Stress, fever, sunlight, or menstruation can trigger reactivation, and the virus travels back down the axon to the skin. For herpes labialis, the ganglion is the trigeminal ganglion. Genital herpes reactivates from sacral dorsal root ganglia, and zoster appears in the dermatome of the affected ganglion. A Tzanck smear of a fresh vesicle shows multinucleated giant cells.
whyNot: Keratinocytes are where the virus replicates during an outbreak, but they are killed or shed. They are not the site of latency.
Memory B cells are the latency site of Epstein-Barr virus, not herpes simplex virus.
Correct.
Herpes simplex virus enters through sensory nerve endings in the skin, not motor neurons. Facial motor neurons do not supply the lip epithelium.

questions.stem: The dermis of her lips and cheeks develops from the same embryonic source as which of the following?
options: Dentin-forming odontoblasts
Enamel-forming ameloblasts
Skeletal muscle of the tongue
Dermis of the lower back
approach: The dermis of the face and much of the head arises from neural crest cells of the head region.
Odontoblasts, which make dentin, are also neural crest derivatives.
The trunk dermis instead arises from somites (dermatomes), and tongue muscle arises from occipital somites.
questions.why: Neural crest cells migrate widely and form melanocytes, Schwann cells, dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, the adrenal medulla, and odontoblasts. In the head they also form most of the facial connective tissue, including the facial dermis, bones of the face, and the dental papilla that becomes dentin and pulp. Below the head, dermis comes from the dermatome portion of the somites, with some contribution from lateral plate mesoderm in the limbs and ventral body wall. So the facial dermis and odontoblasts share an origin, while the dermis of the back does not.
whyNot: Correct.
Ameloblasts make enamel and come from the oral ectoderm that forms the enamel organ, not from neural crest.
Most tongue muscles come from occipital somite myoblasts that are innervated by the hypoglossal nerve. They are paraxial mesoderm.
The dermis of the back arises from the dermatomes of the somites, which is paraxial mesoderm, not neural crest.

case: A 19-year-old man who runs on his college cross-country team comes to the physician because of itchy, prickling bumps that appear within minutes of starting to run, during hot showers, and when he feels anxious. Each episode fades within an hour. He has no lip or tongue swelling, wheezing, or lightheadedness during episodes. He takes no medications. After 10 minutes of running on a treadmill in the office, his temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F), pulse is 132/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 138/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows numerous 2- to 3-mm wheals surrounded by large erythematous flares on the trunk and upper arms. His skin is moist with sweat. Diagnosis: cholinergic urticaria.

questions.stem: His 25-year-old cousin has had recurrent episodes of nonpitting swelling of the face, hands, and once the bowel wall, each lasting 2 to 3 days, without hives or itching. Serum C4 concentration is low. Which of the following mediators most likely causes the cousin's swelling?
options: Bradykinin
Histamine
Leukotriene C4
Prostaglandin D2
approach: Swelling that lasts days, involves deep tissue, and comes without hives or itch is angioedema that does not come from mast cells.
A low C4 points to C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency, because unchecked C1 keeps consuming C4.
C1 inhibitor also controls kallikrein, so its loss lets kallikrein cleave kininogen into bradykinin, which opens venules.
questions.why: Urticaria comes from mast cell degranulation, which releases histamine and other mediators into the superficial dermis and produces itchy wheals that each last less than 24 hours. Angioedema is the same kind of leak in the deep dermis and subcutis. Hereditary angioedema from C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency is different: it causes swelling without hives or itch, lasts days, and can involve the larynx and gut. C1 inhibitor normally blocks kallikrein and factor XIIa, so when it is missing, bradykinin accumulates. Antihistamines do not help, and ACE inhibitors, which slow bradykinin breakdown, must be avoided.
whyNot: Correct.
Histamine from mast cells causes itchy wheals and allergic angioedema. The cousin has no hives and a low C4, which points away from mast cells.
Leukotriene C4 is a mast cell product that contributes to allergic bronchoconstriction and vascular leak. It is not the mediator of complement-linked angioedema.
Prostaglandin D2 is released by mast cells and causes flushing and bronchoconstriction. It is not the mediator in C1 inhibitor deficiency.

questions.stem: The wheals on his trunk represent fluid that has leaked into the superficial dermis within minutes. Which of the following most directly explains this leak?
options: Neutrophil-mediated injury of capillary endothelial cells
Lymphatic obstruction trapping filtered protein in the dermis
Endothelial cell contraction in postcapillary venules
Arteriolar constriction raising capillary hydrostatic pressure
approach: A wheal forms within minutes and fades within hours, so the leak must be fast and reversible.
Histamine from mast cells binds H1 receptors on endothelial cells.
The endothelial cells of postcapillary venules contract, opening gaps between them, so protein-rich fluid escapes into the dermis.
questions.why: Increased vascular permeability is the first step of acute inflammation. Histamine, bradykinin, and leukotrienes make endothelial cells of postcapillary venules contract, which opens gaps between cells within seconds to minutes. The response is short-lived, which fits a wheal that fades within an hour. The surrounding flare is arteriolar dilation through an axon reflex. Later steps of inflammation bring leukocytes to the same venules: selectins mediate rolling, integrins binding ICAM-1 give firm adhesion, PECAM-1 allows transmigration, and C5a, LTB4, and IL-8 guide chemotaxis.
whyNot: Neutrophils can injure endothelium and cause a slower, longer-lasting leak, but they are not present in a wheal that forms within minutes.
Lymphatic obstruction causes slowly developing, persistent lymphedema, not swelling that comes and goes within an hour.
Correct.
Arteriolar constriction would lower capillary pressure and reduce flow. The flare around the wheal shows that arterioles are dilated.

questions.stem: His wheals appear as his core temperature rises and he begins to sweat. The sweat glands responsible for his thermoregulatory sweating are innervated by which of the following?
options: Sympathetic fibers releasing norepinephrine
Sympathetic fibers releasing acetylcholine
Parasympathetic fibers releasing acetylcholine
Somatic motor fibers releasing acetylcholine
approach: Thermoregulatory sweat comes from eccrine glands, which open directly onto the skin over most of the body.
Eccrine glands are innervated by the sympathetic nervous system, but the postganglionic fibers release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors.
In cholinergic urticaria, this acetylcholine-driven sweating response is linked to the hives, which explains the name.
questions.why: Eccrine glands are coiled glands in the deep dermis that open directly onto the skin surface and make watery sweat for cooling. They are an exception in the autonomic system: they receive sympathetic postganglionic fibers that release acetylcholine onto M3 muscarinic receptors. That is why anticholinergic drugs cause dry skin and why botulinum toxin treats hyperhidrosis. Apocrine glands open into hair follicles in the axilla and anogenital area and respond mainly to adrenergic stimulation. Sebaceous glands are holocrine and controlled by androgens rather than nerves.
whyNot: Sympathetic adrenergic fibers drive most sympathetic targets and act on apocrine glands, but eccrine thermoregulatory sweating uses acetylcholine.
Correct.
The skin has essentially no parasympathetic supply. Eccrine glands receive sympathetic fibers even though those fibers release acetylcholine.
Somatic motor fibers release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors of skeletal muscle. They do not supply glands.

questions.stem: His teammate receives a tetanus toxoid booster 2 years after his previous dose. Six hours later, a painful, indurated, erythematous area develops at the injection site and becomes hemorrhagic over the next day. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of the teammate's reaction?
options: IgE cross-linking on sensitized dermal mast cells
IgG binding to keratinocyte surface glycoproteins
Memory T cells releasing cytokines
Local immune complexes activating complement
approach: A frequent booster leaves high levels of circulating IgG against tetanus toxoid.
Injected antigen meets that IgG in the vessel walls of the dermis and forms immune complexes.
Complement activation and neutrophils damage the vessels within hours, which is a type III (Arthus) reaction.
questions.why: The Arthus reaction is a localized type III hypersensitivity. When antigen is injected into a person with high levels of specific IgG, immune complexes form in and around small dermal vessels. They activate complement, releasing C5a, which draws neutrophils that damage vessel walls, causing edema, hemorrhage, and sometimes necrosis about 4 to 12 hours later. Type I reactions such as urticaria appear within minutes, type II reactions involve antibody against fixed tissue antigens such as pemphigus, and type IV reactions such as the tuberculin test peak at 48 to 72 hours.
whyNot: IgE cross-linking on mast cells is type I hypersensitivity, which causes hives or anaphylaxis within minutes, not a hemorrhagic plaque after 6 hours.
IgG binding to fixed tissue antigens is type II hypersensitivity, as in pemphigus. Tetanus toxoid is not a keratinocyte antigen.
Memory T cell reactions are type IV and take 48 to 72 hours to peak, as in the tuberculin skin test.
Correct.

case: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of facial redness for 2 years. She flushes easily, and the redness worsens after hot drinks, red wine, spicy food, and time in the sun. Her eyes often feel gritty. She has never had acne. Her temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows persistent erythema of the central cheeks, nose, chin, and forehead with telangiectasias and scattered papules and pustules. No comedones are present. The eyelid margins are mildly erythematous. There is no joint swelling. Diagnosis: papulopustular rosacea.

questions.stem: If her disease progresses over many years without treatment, which of the following changes of the nose is most likely to develop?
options: Collapse of the nasal bridge from cartilage loss
Perforation of the nasal septum from vasculitis
Thickened nasal skin with sebaceous hyperplasia
Pearly papule with rolled borders on the ala
approach: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory disease of the central face with flushing, persistent erythema, telangiectasias, and papules and pustules.
Long-standing inflammation and vascular leak in the nose lead to fibrosis and enlargement of sebaceous glands.
The result is a bulbous, thickened nose called rhinophyma, which is more common in men but can occur in women.
questions.why: Rosacea begins with flushing triggered by heat, sunlight, alcohol, spicy food, and emotion, and progresses to persistent central facial erythema with telangiectasias. Papules and pustules then appear, without the comedones of acne. In the phymatous form, years of inflammation cause fibrosis and sebaceous gland hyperplasia, most often in the nose (rhinophyma). Ocular rosacea is another complication, with gritty eyes, blepharitis, and conjunctival injection, as her eyelid margins suggest.
whyNot: Saddle-nose collapse comes from destruction of nasal cartilage, as in granulomatosis with polyangiitis, relapsing polychondritis, or congenital syphilis.
Septal perforation occurs with cocaine use or granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not rosacea.
Correct.
A pearly papule with rolled borders is basal cell carcinoma, a result of cumulative UV damage, not of rosacea.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional findings in this patient would most strongly suggest systemic lupus erythematosus rather than rosacea?
options: Greasy yellow scale in the nasolabial folds
Open and closed comedones on the forehead
Flushing within minutes of drinking red wine
Erythema sparing the nasolabial folds
approach: Rosacea, lupus, acne, and seborrheic dermatitis can all cause a red face, so look for the feature that belongs to only one.
The malar rash of lupus covers the cheeks and nasal bridge but characteristically spares the nasolabial folds.
Greasy scale belongs to seborrheic dermatitis, comedones belong to acne, and trigger-linked flushing belongs to rosacea.
questions.why: The butterfly (malar) rash of systemic lupus is a photosensitive erythema over the cheeks and nasal bridge that typically spares the nasolabial folds, and it lacks pustules. Rosacea has central facial erythema with flushing triggers, telangiectasias, papules, and pustules without comedones. Acne vulgaris begins in adolescence and is defined by comedones. Seborrheic dermatitis causes greasy yellow scale in the nasolabial folds, eyebrows, and scalp. Each condition has a feature that sets it apart.
whyNot: Greasy yellow scale in the nasolabial folds and eyebrows is seborrheic dermatitis, which often coexists with rosacea but is not lupus.
Comedones are the primary lesion of acne vulgaris. Their presence points to acne, not lupus.
Flushing after alcohol, heat, or spicy food is a classic rosacea trigger and supports her current diagnosis.
Correct.

questions.stem: On a hot day, as her core temperature rises, her skin vessels dilate and she begins to sweat. Which of the following brain regions integrates the rise in core temperature and drives these heat loss responses?
options: Preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus
Posterior hypothalamus near the mammillary bodies
Ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus
Supraoptic nucleus above the optic chiasm
approach: Heat loss responses are cutaneous vasodilation and sweating.
The hypothalamus compares core and skin temperature input with a set point.
The preoptic anterior hypothalamus drives heat loss, and the posterior hypothalamus drives heat conservation and heat production.
questions.why: Core temperature is sensed by warm-sensitive neurons in the preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus, which also receive input from skin thermoreceptors. When temperature rises above the set point, this region reduces sympathetic tone to skin arterioles, causing vasodilation, and activates sympathetic cholinergic fibers to eccrine glands, causing sweating. When temperature falls, the posterior hypothalamus drives vasoconstriction, piloerection, and shivering. A lesion of the anterior hypothalamus causes hyperthermia, and a lesion of the posterior hypothalamus causes poor tolerance of cold.
whyNot: Correct.
The posterior hypothalamus drives heat conservation and production, such as vasoconstriction and shivering. It is not the heat loss center.
The ventromedial nucleus is a satiety center. Lesions cause overeating and obesity, not loss of heat responses.
The supraoptic nucleus makes antidiuretic hormone for water balance. It does not control skin blood flow or sweating.

topics: Heat loss and heat gain centers

questions.stem: Ultraviolet light, one of her triggers, generates reactive oxygen species in the skin, including superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. Which of the following reactions produces the hydroxyl radical, the most damaging of these species?
options: Breakdown of hydrogen peroxide by catalase
Reaction of hydrogen peroxide with ferrous iron
Dismutation of superoxide by superoxide dismutase
Reduction of hydrogen peroxide by glutathione peroxidase
approach: Superoxide is converted to hydrogen peroxide, which is not itself a radical.
Hydrogen peroxide becomes far more dangerous when it meets a transition metal such as Fe2+.
Fe2+ plus hydrogen peroxide gives Fe3+, hydroxide, and the hydroxyl radical. This is the Fenton reaction.
questions.why: Reactive oxygen species form from electron leak in mitochondria, from NADPH oxidase in phagocytes, and from UV and ionizing radiation. Superoxide is converted to hydrogen peroxide by superoxide dismutase. In the presence of free ferrous iron, hydrogen peroxide undergoes the Fenton reaction to form the hydroxyl radical, the most reactive species. Hydroxyl radicals start lipid peroxidation of membranes, oxidize proteins, and break DNA strands. Oxidative stress from UV exposure is thought to contribute to the inflammation of rosacea.
whyNot: Catalase breaks hydrogen peroxide down to water and oxygen, which removes it safely rather than making radicals.
Correct.
Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen. It is a protective step and does not make hydroxyl radicals.
Glutathione peroxidase reduces hydrogen peroxide to water using glutathione. It is an antioxidant defense.

topics: Reactive oxygen species and antioxidant enzymes

dx: Oral and cutaneous lichen planus with chronic hepatitis C
case: A 52-year-old woman who works as a nurse comes to the physician because of an itchy rash on her wrists and shins for 3 months and a burning sensation in her mouth when she eats spicy food. Twenty-five years ago, she had a needle-stick injury from a hollow-bore needle used on a patient of unknown infection status and was not tested afterward. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows flat-topped, violaceous, polygonal papules on the flexor wrists and shins, with fine white lines on their surfaces. A lacy white network is present on both buccal mucosae and cannot be scraped off. Serum alanine aminotransferase activity is 68 U/L (7 to 35). Anti-hepatitis C virus antibody is positive, and hepatitis C virus RNA is detected. Diagnosis: oral and cutaneous lichen planus associated with chronic hepatitis C.

questions.stem: A biopsy specimen of a papule on her wrist would most likely show which of the following?
options: Spongiosis with small intraepidermal vesicles
Regular acanthosis with neutrophils in the parakeratotic scale
Subepidermal blister with many eosinophils
Bandlike T cell infiltrate with sawtooth rete ridges
approach: Purple, polygonal, planar, pruritic papules with white lines (Wickham striae) are lichen planus.
Lichen planus is an interface dermatitis driven by T cells attacking basal keratinocytes.
A dense band of lymphocytes hugs the dermal-epidermal junction, and damage to the basal layer reshapes the rete ridges into a sawtooth pattern.
questions.why: Lichen planus is a T cell-mediated attack on basal keratinocytes. Biopsy shows a dense, bandlike lymphocytic infiltrate along the dermal-epidermal junction, vacuolar damage to the basal layer, hypergranulosis, and pointed, sawtooth rete ridges. Dead basal keratinocytes appear as round eosinophilic Civatte (colloid) bodies. Clinically, the papules are pruritic, purple, polygonal, and planar, with Wickham striae on the surface. Oral lesions are a lacy white network, and lichen planus has a well-known association with hepatitis C infection.
whyNot: Spongiosis with vesicles is the eczematous pattern of contact or atopic dermatitis, not the purple flat papules of lichen planus.
Regular acanthosis with neutrophils in parakeratotic scale (Munro microabscesses) is psoriasis, which forms silvery-scaled plaques.
A subepidermal blister with eosinophils is bullous pemphigoid, which forms tense bullae.
Correct.

topics: The six Ps of lichen planus

questions.stem: Her 58-year-old brother has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years and drinks heavily. He has a painless, sharply demarcated, 2-cm white plaque on the floor of his mouth that cannot be scraped off. He has no other skin or mucosal lesions, and HIV testing is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in the brother?
options: Oral leukoplakia
Oral hairy leukoplakia
Pseudomembranous candidiasis
Reticular lichen planus
approach: A white plaque that cannot be scraped off rules out thrush, which wipes away.
A single sharply demarcated plaque on the floor of the mouth in a heavy smoker and drinker, with negative HIV testing, fits leukoplakia.
Lichen planus forms a lacy, bilateral network, and hairy leukoplakia forms corrugated plaques on the lateral tongue in immunosuppressed patients.
questions.why: Leukoplakia is a clinical term for a white oral plaque that cannot be scraped off and has no other specific cause. It is strongly linked to tobacco and alcohol use. Biopsy may show only hyperkeratosis or may show dysplasia, and a fraction of lesions progress to squamous cell carcinoma, especially on the floor of the mouth and ventral tongue. For that reason, every leukoplakia should be biopsied. Oral hairy leukoplakia is caused by Epstein-Barr virus in immunosuppressed patients and is not premalignant.
whyNot: Correct.
Oral hairy leukoplakia causes corrugated white plaques on the lateral tongue in patients with HIV or other immunosuppression. It is caused by Epstein-Barr virus.
Thrush forms creamy white patches that scrape off and leave a red base. The brother's plaque cannot be scraped off.
Reticular lichen planus forms a bilateral, lacy white network on the buccal mucosa, like his sister's. A single solid plaque on the floor of the mouth does not fit.

topics: White lesions of the oral cavity

questions.stem: Assume her needle-stick source patient had been infected with hepatitis B virus (HBeAg positive), hepatitis C virus, and HIV, and that she was not immune to hepatitis B at the time. Which of the following ranks her risk of acquiring each infection from that single injury, from highest to lowest?
options: Hepatitis C virus, hepatitis B virus, HIV
Hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, HIV
HIV, hepatitis C virus, hepatitis B virus
Hepatitis B virus, HIV, hepatitis C virus
approach: Transmission risk after a needle stick depends mostly on how much virus is in the blood.
Hepatitis B, especially when the source is HBeAg positive, reaches very high blood levels, so the risk can be 30% or more.
Hepatitis C carries a risk of about 2%, and HIV about 0.3%.
questions.why: Hepatitis B virus is the most transmissible bloodborne pathogen after a percutaneous injury. With an HBeAg-positive source and a nonimmune worker, the risk of clinical hepatitis is about 22 to 31%, and the risk of any infection is higher still, which is why hepatitis B vaccination is required for health care workers. Hepatitis C transmits in about 1 to 2% of exposures, and HIV in about 0.3%. Risk rises with a hollow-bore needle that carries blood inside it, a deep injury, visible blood on the device, and a high viral load in the source.
whyNot: Hepatitis C transmission after a needle stick is about 2%, well below the risk from an HBeAg-positive hepatitis B source.
Correct.
HIV has the lowest transmission risk of the three, about 0.3% after a percutaneous exposure.
Hepatitis B is the highest, but HIV is lower than hepatitis C, not higher.

topics: Hepatitis B vaccination for health care workers

questions.stem: Her biopsy specimen also shows round, eosinophilic, anucleate bodies near the dermal-epidermal junction with no surrounding neutrophils. Which of the following mechanisms most directly produced these bodies?
options: Membrane attack complex lysis after antibody binding
ATP depletion with cell swelling and membrane rupture
Granzyme B delivered through perforin pores
Inflammasome activation of caspase 1
approach: These are Civatte bodies, which are basal keratinocytes that died by apoptosis.
Shrunken, eosinophilic cells with no inflammation around them mean apoptosis, not necrosis.
In lichen planus, CD8 cytotoxic T cells trigger apoptosis by releasing perforin and granzyme B, which activates caspases inside the target cell.
questions.why: Cytotoxic T cells kill target cells in two main ways. They release perforin, which forms pores in the target membrane, and granzyme B, which enters through them and activates caspases. They can also use Fas ligand to engage Fas and activate caspase 8, which is the extrinsic pathway. The intrinsic pathway instead starts inside the cell, when BCL-2 family proteins allow cytochrome c to leave the mitochondria and activate caspase 9. Apoptotic cells shrink, condense their nuclei, and break into apoptotic bodies that are removed without inflammation. Necrosis causes swelling, rupture, and inflammation.
whyNot: Complement lysis after antibody binding is a type II mechanism. It causes cells to swell and burst, and lichen planus is not antibody mediated.
ATP depletion with swelling and rupture is necrosis, which provokes inflammation. These bodies are shrunken and have no inflammation around them.
Correct.
Inflammasome activation of caspase 1 causes pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death that releases IL-1 beta.

dx: Erythrodermic psoriasis with psoriatic nail pitting
case: A 60-year-old man is admitted to the hospital from the emergency department because of generalized redness and scaling of his skin for 1 week, with chills. He has had plaque psoriasis on his elbows, knees, and scalp for 20 years. A course of oral prednisone prescribed for a flare was stopped abruptly 10 days ago. His temperature is 36.0 °C (96.8 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg. Physical examination shows erythema with fine scale covering more than 90% of his body surface. The fingernails show many small pits, distal separation of the nail plate from the nail bed, and yellow-brown oil-drop discoloration. Diagnosis: erythrodermic psoriasis with psoriatic nail disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following cytokine pathways is most central to the keratinocyte hyperproliferation in his disease?
options: IL-4 and IL-13 release by Th2 cells
IL-23 sustaining IL-17 release by Th17 cells
IL-5 release by Th2 cells recruiting eosinophils
IL-10 and TGF-beta release by regulatory T cells
approach: Psoriasis is a T cell-mediated disease with genetic risk (HLA-Cw6) and triggers such as trauma (Koebner phenomenon), infection, and steroid withdrawal.
Dendritic cells in the skin release IL-23, which expands and maintains Th17 cells.
IL-17 and IL-22 from Th17 cells drive keratinocyte hyperproliferation, and TNF amplifies the inflammation.
questions.why: In psoriasis, activated dermal dendritic cells make IL-23, which maintains Th17 cells. These cells release IL-17 and IL-22, which make keratinocytes divide rapidly and produce chemokines and antimicrobial peptides that draw in more neutrophils and T cells. TNF amplifies the loop. This explains why biologic drugs that block TNF, IL-17, or IL-23 work so well. Clinically, psoriasis causes silvery-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces and scalp, nail pitting, and in some patients psoriatic arthritis. Abrupt withdrawal of systemic steroids can trigger erythrodermic or pustular flares.
whyNot: IL-4 and IL-13 from Th2 cells drive atopic dermatitis, the barrier-related itchy eczema of atopic patients.
Correct.
IL-5 recruits and activates eosinophils, as in asthma and parasitic infection. Psoriatic plaques are rich in neutrophils and T cells, not eosinophils.
IL-10 and TGF-beta are suppressive cytokines that dampen inflammation. They do not drive keratinocyte proliferation.

topics: IL-23 and Th17 axis in psoriasis

questions.stem: Before this episode, scraping the scale from a plaque on his elbow produced pinpoint bleeding. Which of the following histologic features best explains this finding?
options: Neutrophil collections within the parakeratotic scale
Uniformly elongated rete ridges with acanthosis
Thin suprapapillary plates over dilated capillaries
Reduced or absent stratum granulosum
approach: Pinpoint bleeding after removing scale is the Auspitz sign.
For bleeding to occur, blood vessels must sit very close to the surface.
In psoriasis, the dermal papillae extend upward with dilated, tortuous capillaries, and the epidermis above each papilla (the suprapapillary plate) is thinned.
questions.why: Psoriasis has a characteristic histology: acanthosis with regularly elongated rete ridges, parakeratosis (retained nuclei in the stratum corneum), a thin or absent stratum granulosum, and neutrophil collections in the stratum corneum (Munro microabscesses). The dermal papillae are tall, with dilated, tortuous capillaries, and the epidermis over the tips of the papillae is thin. When the scale is lifted off, only a few cell layers separate the capillaries from the surface, so they tear and bleed in tiny points. That is the Auspitz sign.
whyNot: Munro microabscesses are a classic psoriasis finding, but neutrophils in the scale do not explain bleeding when the scale is removed.
Elongated rete ridges thicken the epidermis between papillae. They do not put vessels near the surface.
Correct.
Loss of the granular layer explains the defective keratinization and parakeratotic scale. It does not explain bleeding.

questions.stem: The pits in his fingernail plates most likely reflect psoriatic involvement of which of the following parts of the nail unit?
options: Nail bed beneath the plate
Hyponychium under the free edge
Lateral nail fold
Proximal nail matrix
approach: Pits are small defects on the upper surface of the nail plate.
The nail plate is made by the matrix, and the proximal matrix forms the top (dorsal) layer of the plate.
Psoriatic foci in the proximal matrix shed clusters of abnormal cells that leave pits as the plate grows out.
questions.why: The nail unit has a matrix under the proximal nail fold that makes the nail plate, a nail bed that the plate rests on, a hyponychium under the free edge, and proximal and lateral folds that frame the plate. The proximal part of the matrix makes the dorsal plate surface, so psoriasis there causes pits. Psoriasis in the nail bed causes oil-drop discoloration, subungual hyperkeratosis, and onycholysis, which he also has. An ingrown nail occurs when the plate grows into the lateral nail fold.
whyNot: Nail bed disease causes oil-drop spots, splinter hemorrhages, and onycholysis. The nail bed does not form the plate surface, so it does not cause pits.
The hyponychium seals the space under the free edge. Disease there causes subungual hyperkeratosis and lifting, not pits.
The lateral nail fold borders the plate. It is the site of ingrown nails and paronychia, not pitting.
Correct.

questions.stem: During a heat wave, the air in his room reaches 38 °C (100.4 °F), which is higher than his skin temperature. Which of the following is the only route by which he can still lose heat to the environment?
options: Evaporation of water from skin
Radiation to surrounding surfaces
Conduction to the bed surface
Convection to the moving room air
approach: Radiation, conduction, and convection all move heat from a warmer object to a cooler one.
When the environment is warmer than the skin, these routes reverse and the body gains heat.
Evaporation removes heat as water changes to vapor, so it still works when the air is hotter than the skin.
questions.why: At rest in a cool room, most heat is lost by radiation, with smaller amounts by conduction, convection, and evaporation. The first three depend on a temperature gradient from skin to surroundings. When ambient temperature rises above skin temperature, the gradient reverses and the body absorbs heat by those routes. Evaporation of sweat and water from skin is then the only way to lose heat. High humidity slows evaporation, which is why humid heat is so dangerous, and patients with extensive skin disease such as erythroderma are especially vulnerable to temperature swings.
whyNot: Correct.
Radiation sends heat to cooler surfaces. When surroundings are warmer than skin, he gains heat by radiation.
Conduction moves heat to a cooler object in contact. A bed at room temperature above skin temperature would add heat.
Convection carries heat away only if the moving air is cooler than the skin. Here the air is warmer, so convection adds heat.

topics: Heat loss in hot and humid environments

case: A newborn girl in the neonatal intensive care unit is evaluated for blisters that were present at birth. She was born at 39 weeks' gestation to healthy parents who are first cousins. Her 4-year-old brother is healthy. Physical examination shows blisters and erosions on the hands, feet, knees, and elbows, and new blisters form at sites of handling and where the diaper rubs. Oral erosions are present, and several toenails are thickened and dystrophic. Older erosions are healing with atrophic scars and small white cysts. Immunofluorescence mapping of a skin biopsy specimen shows that the blister forms beneath the lamina densa. Diagnosis: recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa.

questions.stem: A mutation in the gene for which of the following proteins is most likely responsible for her disease?
options: Type VII collagen
Keratins 5 and 14
Laminin 332
Type XVII collagen
approach: The split is beneath the lamina densa, at the level of the anchoring fibrils, and the blisters heal with scars and milia.
Anchoring fibrils are made of type VII collagen, which ties the lamina densa to the papillary dermis.
Loss of type VII collagen (COL7A1 mutations) causes dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa.
questions.why: Epidermolysis bullosa types are defined by where the skin splits, which depends on the defective protein. In the simplex type, mutations in keratins 5 and 14 make basal keratinocytes fragile, so the split is within the basal cells. In the junctional type, defects in laminin 332 or collagen XVII separate the skin through the lamina lucida. In the dystrophic type, defective type VII collagen weakens anchoring fibrils, so the split is below the lamina densa. Because this split is in the dermis, blisters heal with scarring and milia.
whyNot: Correct.
Keratin 5 and 14 mutations cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex, with a split within basal keratinocytes that usually heals without scarring. It is usually autosomal dominant.
Laminin 332 defects cause junctional epidermolysis bullosa, with a split in the lamina lucida above the lamina densa.
Collagen XVII (BP180) defects also cause junctional epidermolysis bullosa through the lamina lucida. This protein is the target of autoantibodies in bullous pemphigoid.

questions.stem: As she grows older, she is at greatest risk of developing which of the following malignancies?
options: Melanoma arising in a congenital nevus
Basal cell carcinoma on the sun-exposed face
Cutaneous T cell lymphoma of the trunk
Squamous cell carcinoma in chronic wounds
approach: In recessive dystrophic disease, blisters break down into chronic wounds that heal with scars, over and over.
Repeated wounding and scarring create an environment that promotes keratinocyte cancer.
These patients develop aggressive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, often by early adulthood, and it is a major cause of death.
questions.why: Recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa begins at birth with blisters from minor friction. The skin, mouth, esophagus, and nails are involved. Cycles of blistering and scarring cause mitten deformities with fused fingers and toes, joint contractures, esophageal strictures, and loss of nails. The most serious long-term complication is squamous cell carcinoma arising in chronic wounds and scars. These cancers appear in adolescence or early adulthood, grow aggressively, and spread early.
whyNot: Melanoma in a large congenital nevus is a separate risk that does not depend on blistering disease.
Basal cell carcinoma is driven by cumulative UV exposure and is not the cancer linked to chronic wounds in epidermolysis bullosa.
Cutaneous T cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides) arises from skin-homing T cells and is not linked to epidermolysis bullosa.
Correct.

topics: Complications of recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa
Squamous cell carcinoma in chronic wounds

questions.stem: Her parents are both heterozygous carriers of the disease-causing mutation. Which of the following is the probability that her healthy 4-year-old brother is a carrier?
approach: Healthy parents with an affected child, plus consanguinity, point to autosomal recessive inheritance with both parents as carriers.
A carrier-by-carrier cross gives 1/4 unaffected noncarrier, 1/2 carrier, and 1/4 affected.
The brother is known to be unaffected, so remove the affected 1/4. Of the remaining 3/4, carriers make up 2/4, so his risk is 2/3.
questions.why: When both parents are carriers of an autosomal recessive mutation, each child has a 1/4 chance of being affected, 1/2 of being a carrier, and 1/4 of being a noncarrier. Once a sibling is known to be unaffected, the affected outcome is no longer possible, so the denominator becomes 3/4. His chance of being a carrier is (1/2) divided by (3/4), which equals 2/3. Each new pregnancy for these parents still has a 1/4 chance of an affected child. Autosomal dominant skin disorders such as neurofibromatosis type 1 and epidermolysis bullosa simplex instead give a 1/2 risk to each child of an affected parent.
whyNot: 1/4 is the chance that any child of two carriers is affected. It is not his carrier risk given that he is healthy.
1/2 is the carrier risk for a child of two carriers before anything is known about the child. Knowing he is unaffected raises it.
Correct.
3/4 is the chance that a child of two carriers is unaffected, not the chance that a healthy child is a carrier.

topics: Carrier probability in an unaffected sibling

questions.stem: Another infant in the unit, born at term, is covered with a white, greasy coating at birth. This coating is composed mainly of which of the following?
options: Maternal IgG deposited on the fetal skin surface
Sebum mixed with shed periderm and keratinocytes
Eccrine sweat mixed with amniotic fluid proteins
Apocrine secretions trapped in the lanugo hair
approach: The white, greasy coating on a newborn is vernix caseosa.
Fetal sebaceous glands become active late in gestation under the influence of maternal and fetal hormones.
Their sebum mixes with desquamated periderm and keratinocytes, and lanugo hair helps hold the coating on the skin.
questions.why: The fetal epidermis starts as a single layer covered by the periderm, a temporary outer layer that is shed as the epidermis stratifies. Melanoblasts migrate in from the neural crest, and hair buds grow down into the dermis over dermal papillae to form hair follicles. Fine lanugo hair covers the fetus in the second half of pregnancy. Sebaceous glands bud from the hair follicles and secrete sebum, which combines with shed periderm and keratinocytes to form vernix caseosa. Vernix protects the skin from amniotic fluid and helps with barrier function and temperature control after birth.
whyNot: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta into the fetal blood. It does not form a coating on the skin.
Correct.
Eccrine glands are not yet secreting much sweat at birth, and vernix is lipid rich, not watery.
Apocrine glands become active at puberty. They do not make vernix.

case: An 82-year-old man in a nursing home, bedbound since a stroke 1 year ago, is evaluated for an intensely itchy rash with blisters for 3 weeks. His temperature is 36.7 °C (98.1 °F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 132/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows tense bullae 1 to 3 cm in diameter filled with clear fluid, many arising on red, urticarial plaques of the inner thighs, flexor forearms, and lower abdomen. Nikolsky sign is negative. There are no oral lesions. Over the sacrum, there is a 3-cm ulcer with full-thickness skin loss and visible subcutaneous fat. No bone, tendon, or muscle is visible. Diagnosis: bullous pemphigoid.

questions.stem: Which of the following most directly causes the epidermis to separate from the dermis in his blistering disease?
options: IgG to desmosomes directly blocking cell adhesion
Cytotoxic T cells killing basal keratinocytes
IgG to hemidesmosomes with complement and eosinophils
IgA deposits in dermal papillae attracting neutrophils
approach: Tense bullae on urticarial plaques in an older adult, with a negative Nikolsky sign and no oral lesions, are bullous pemphigoid.
The target antigens are the hemidesmosomal proteins BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230, which anchor basal cells to the basement membrane.
Bound IgG activates complement, which recruits eosinophils and neutrophils whose proteases cut through the lamina lucida.
questions.why: Bullous pemphigoid is a type II hypersensitivity in which IgG autoantibodies bind BP180 and BP230 in hemidesmosomes. The antibodies cause most of their damage through inflammation rather than by blocking adhesion directly. They activate complement, and the inflammatory cells that arrive, especially eosinophils, release proteases that split the skin in the lamina lucida. The full-thickness epidermis forms the blister roof, so bullae are tense and rarely rupture. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane. It mainly affects people over 70, and oral lesions are uncommon.
whyNot: Antibodies against desmosomal desmogleins cause pemphigus, which forms fragile intraepidermal blisters and a positive Nikolsky sign.
Cytotoxic T cells killing keratinocytes is the mechanism of erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, not autoimmune bullae with eosinophils.
Correct.
IgA deposits in dermal papillae with neutrophils describe dermatitis herpetiformis, which forms tiny, intensely itchy vesicles on extensor surfaces with celiac disease.

topics: Type II hypersensitivity in the skin

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman at another facility has crusted, scaly erosions on her scalp, face, and upper chest. Intact blisters are rarely seen because they are very superficial and break easily. Nikolsky sign is positive, and there are no oral lesions. Her autoantibodies target desmoglein 1. At which of the following levels does her skin most likely split?
options: Just above the basal layer of keratinocytes
Subcorneal, within the granular layer
In the lamina lucida of the basement membrane
Below the lamina densa in the upper dermis
approach: Superficial crusted erosions on the seborrheic areas, no mucosal disease, and antibodies to desmoglein 1 are pemphigus foliaceus.
Desmoglein 1 is most strongly expressed in the upper epidermis, while desmoglein 3 is concentrated in the lower layers and mucosa.
Loss of desmoglein 1 adhesion splits the epidermis high, just below the stratum corneum.
questions.why: Pemphigus vulgaris targets desmoglein 3 (often desmoglein 1 too), splits just above the basal layer, and starts with painful oral erosions. Pemphigus foliaceus targets desmoglein 1 only, splits in the granular layer, and spares the mucosa because desmoglein 3 holds mucosal cells together. Both have a positive Nikolsky sign and net-like intercellular IgG on immunofluorescence. Bullous pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomes, splits beneath the epidermis, gives tense bullae with a negative Nikolsky sign, and shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane.
whyNot: A split just above the basal layer is pemphigus vulgaris, which targets desmoglein 3 and almost always involves the mouth.
Correct.
A lamina lucida split is bullous pemphigoid or junctional epidermolysis bullosa. It gives tense blisters and a negative Nikolsky sign.
A split below the lamina densa is dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa or epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, from loss of type VII collagen function.

topics: Pemphigus vulgaris versus pemphigus foliaceus versus bullous pemphigoid

questions.stem: In his blisters, the split occurs through the lamina lucida. Which of the following structures forms the uppermost layer of the blister floor?
options: Lamina densa rich in type IV collagen
Basal keratinocytes joined by desmosomes
Anchoring fibrils of type VII collagen
Papillary dermis rich in type III collagen
approach: From top to bottom, the junction is basal keratinocyte with hemidesmosomes, then lamina lucida, then lamina densa, then anchoring fibrils and dermis.
A split through the lamina lucida leaves the basal cells and hemidesmosomes in the roof.
The first layer below the split is the lamina densa, made mostly of type IV collagen.
questions.why: The dermal-epidermal junction has distinct layers. Basal keratinocytes attach through hemidesmosomes containing BP180 (collagen XVII), BP230, and integrin alpha6 beta4. Below them, the lamina lucida contains laminin 332 and the anchoring filaments of collagen XVII. The lamina densa is a sheet of type IV collagen. Anchoring fibrils of type VII collagen loop from the lamina densa into the papillary dermis. A lamina lucida split, as in bullous pemphigoid and junctional epidermolysis bullosa, places the lamina densa in the floor. That is why antibodies to BP180 stain the roof on salt-split skin. A split below the lamina densa occurs in dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa.
whyNot: Correct.
Basal keratinocytes sit above the lamina lucida, so they form the bottom of the blister roof, not the floor.
Anchoring fibrils lie below the lamina densa. They are in the floor, but deeper, not the uppermost layer.
The papillary dermis lies beneath the lamina densa and anchoring fibrils, so it is deeper in the floor.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would indicate that his sacral ulcer has progressed to the next stage?
options: Nonblanching erythema of intact skin
Partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis
Undermining with tunneling into the fat
Exposed bone, tendon, or muscle
approach: Full-thickness skin loss with visible fat but no bone, tendon, or muscle is a stage 3 pressure injury.
Stage 4 adds exposure of deeper structures: bone, tendon, muscle, ligament, or cartilage.
Undermining and tunneling can occur in both stage 3 and stage 4, so they do not define the next stage.
questions.why: Pressure injuries form when sustained pressure and shear over a bony prominence, such as the sacrum, close capillaries and cause ischemia. Muscle and fat are more sensitive to ischemia than skin, so damage may be deeper than it looks. Stage 1 is nonblanching erythema of intact skin. Stage 2 is partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis. Stage 3 is full-thickness skin loss with visible fat. Stage 4 is full-thickness loss with exposed bone, tendon, muscle, ligament, or cartilage. Immobility, poor nutrition, moisture, and loss of sensation all raise risk, as in this bedbound patient.
whyNot: Nonblanching erythema of intact skin is stage 1, the earliest stage. His ulcer is already past it.
Partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis is stage 2. His ulcer already shows full-thickness loss.
Undermining and tunneling can be present in stage 3 or stage 4. They do not by themselves mark the next stage.
Correct.

case: A 48-year-old woman is referred to a dermatologist because of painful mouth sores for 2 months and blisters on her skin for 3 weeks. The mouth sores began first and have made eating difficult. The skin blisters are soft, break easily, and leave raw, painful areas. She takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows extensive erosions of the buccal mucosa, gingiva, and palate. Flaccid bullae and large erosions are present on the scalp, chest, and back. Gentle lateral pressure on normal-appearing skin next to a blister shears off the epidermis. Diagnosis: pemphigus vulgaris.

questions.stem: Direct immunofluorescence of a biopsy specimen of skin next to a blister would most likely show which of the following patterns?
options: Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane
Granular IgA in the dermal papillae
Granular IgG and C3 in a band at the junction
Intercellular IgG in a net-like pattern
approach: Early painful oral erosions, flaccid bullae, and a positive Nikolsky sign are pemphigus vulgaris.
The autoantibodies are IgG against desmoglein 3 (often also desmoglein 1), which sit on the surfaces of keratinocytes at desmosomes.
Staining outlines every keratinocyte, giving a fishnet or chicken-wire pattern.
questions.why: In pemphigus vulgaris, IgG binds desmogleins on the surface of keratinocytes throughout the epidermis. Direct immunofluorescence therefore shows IgG (often with C3) outlining each cell in a net-like intercellular pattern. Biopsy shows suprabasal acantholysis with a single row of basal cells still attached to the basement membrane, the tombstone pattern. The blisters are thin-roofed and flaccid, and the oral mucosa is usually involved first, often for months before skin lesions appear.
whyNot: Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane is bullous pemphigoid, in which antibodies bind hemidesmosomes.
Granular IgA in the dermal papillae is dermatitis herpetiformis, linked to celiac disease.
A granular band of IgG and C3 at the junction is the lupus band seen in cutaneous lupus erythematosus.
Correct.

questions.stem: Early in her illness, her autoantibodies were directed only against desmoglein 3, and she had oral erosions without skin blisters. Which of the following best explains why her skin was spared at that stage?
options: Desmoglein 1 in skin maintains adhesion when desmoglein 3 fails
Mucosal epithelium lacks the protective stratum corneum
Skin keratinocytes adhere by E-cadherin in place of desmogleins
IgG cannot pass the dermal basement membrane into skin
approach: Desmosomes link neighboring keratinocytes through the cadherins desmoglein and desmocollin.
Oral mucosa relies mainly on desmoglein 3, while skin also expresses abundant desmoglein 1.
When only desmoglein 3 is blocked, desmoglein 1 keeps skin cells attached, so blisters form only in the mouth until antibodies to desmoglein 1 appear.
questions.why: Keratinocytes are joined to each other by desmosomes, built from desmogleins and desmocollins that link to keratin filaments. Adherens junctions use E-cadherin and link to actin. Hemidesmosomes attach basal cells to the basement membrane through BP180, BP230, and integrin alpha6 beta4. Desmoglein 3 dominates in mucosa, and desmoglein 1 is abundant in skin, especially the upper layers. Antibodies against desmoglein 3 alone therefore cause mucosal disease, and adding antibodies to desmoglein 1 brings skin blisters. Antibodies to desmoglein 1 alone cause pemphigus foliaceus with superficial skin blisters and no mucosal lesions. Antibodies to hemidesmosomes cause bullous pemphigoid.
whyNot: Correct.
Lacking a stratum corneum does not change cell-to-cell adhesion. The antibodies act at desmosomes in the living layers of both tissues.
Skin keratinocytes do have adherens junctions with E-cadherin, but they also rely on desmosomes. E-cadherin does not replace desmogleins.
IgG crosses the basement membrane into the epidermis easily. Her later skin blisters show that the antibodies reach the skin.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy has fever and diffuse, tender erythema followed by superficial flaccid blisters that wrinkle and peel with light pressure. The mouth and eyes are spared. A culture of fluid from a blister is sterile, and a nasal swab grows Staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following best explains his blistering?
options: Autoantibody binding to desmoglein 3
Toxin cleavage of desmoglein 1
Superantigen activation of many T cells
Bacterial invasion of the spinous layer
approach: Diffuse tender erythema with superficial peeling in a young child, sterile blister fluid, and a distant staphylococcal focus point to staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.
The skin damage comes from a circulating toxin, not from bacteria in the skin.
Exfoliative toxins A and B are serine proteases that cut desmoglein 1, splitting the epidermis in the granular layer.
questions.why: In staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, Staphylococcus aureus grows at a distant site, such as the nose, conjunctiva, or umbilicus, and releases exfoliative toxins into the blood. The toxins cleave desmoglein 1, the same protein targeted by antibodies in pemphigus foliaceus, so the split is high in the epidermis and the mucosa is spared. Young children are affected because their kidneys clear the toxin poorly. This differs from superantigen diseases such as toxic shock syndrome, where TSST-1 or streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins activate large numbers of T cells and cause diffuse rash, fever, and shock.
whyNot: Autoantibodies to desmoglein 3 cause pemphigus vulgaris, which begins in the mouth. This child's mucosa is spared and his illness is linked to infection.
Correct.
Superantigens activate many T cells and cause toxic shock syndrome with fever, hypotension, and a diffuse rash that desquamates later. They do not cleave desmosomes.
Direct invasion would give a positive blister culture, as in bullous impetigo. His blister fluid is sterile because the toxin acts from a distance.

questions.stem: Which of the following histologic terms describes the change that allows her epidermis to shear off with gentle lateral pressure?
options: Spongiosis
Parakeratosis
Acantholysis
Dyskeratosis
approach: A positive Nikolsky sign means the keratinocytes are no longer held firmly to each other.
Loss of cohesion between keratinocytes because their connections fail is called acantholysis.
In pemphigus, antibodies against desmogleins cause acantholysis, so a sideways push separates the layers.
questions.why: Acantholysis is loss of attachment between keratinocytes after desmosomes fail, leaving rounded, separated cells inside a blister. It defines pemphigus. Acanthosis is thickening of the spinous layer, as in psoriasis. Hyperkeratosis is a thickened stratum corneum, and parakeratosis is retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum, as in psoriasis. Spongiosis is edema between keratinocytes, as in eczema and contact dermatitis. Dyskeratosis is abnormal early keratinization of individual cells below the granular layer, as in squamous cell carcinoma in situ.
whyNot: Spongiosis is edema between keratinocytes in eczematous dermatitis. The cells stay connected by stretched desmosomes.
Parakeratosis is retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum from rapid turnover, as in psoriasis. It does not weaken adhesion.
Correct.
Dyskeratosis is premature keratinization of single cells. It does not cause the epidermis to shear off.
